title: The newest years are always missing
context: Every chart on these pages stops at the last year its publisher has counted, between four months and three and a half years behind today.
ask: When a chart's last year shows a fall, is it a real fall or a count that is not finished?
unit: Months between a source's latest data and November 2026

rows.about: Counted from every community prescription dispensed in England, so it is complete within months. The annual release each July covers the financial year to March.
A national household interview survey run all year; CDC publishes the year's estimates the following summer.
Death certificates counted as they arrive. Provisional figures cover all causes within months but rise as late certificates and pending investigations are added.
The complete US death file for a year, published after every certificate is coded: about a year and a half later.
WHO's modelled estimates for every country on one method. They wait for countries' own records, then for the modelling: about three years.
A survey with a physical exam and a check of the medicines in the home, run in multi-year cycles; the newest cycle ended in 2023.
Every primary brain tumour reported to US cancer registries, published as five-year averages about three years after the last year.
Every new cancer reported to state registries; cases take time to be confirmed and coded, so the newest year is about three and a half years old.

caption: How far each source's newest figures lag behind November 2026. A chart's last year is the latest year a publisher has counted, not the latest year that happened.
entered_from: each publisher's release page, read 20 November 2026
